extracted.intended_audience: writers, editors, copyeditors, journalists, and students seeking guidance on word usage and grammar
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for correct word choice, spelling, grammar, and idiom usage in standard written English; entries are short usage rules contrasting commonly confused words and recommending preferred forms. Useful for copyediting and improving formal prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: use of 'literally'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using literally loosely in figurative senses (e.g., they were literally glued to their seats) unless the literal sense actually applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wherever guides have accepted this usage, they should be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: loathe vs loath
rubrics_metrics.description: To loathe (verb) means to detest intensely; loath (adjective) means reluctant or unwilling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciations differ: loathe (th as in 'that'), loath (th as in 'thing'). Example: 'I loathe tabloid television' vs 'Tracy seems loath to admit mistakes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: lose vs loose vs loosen
rubrics_metrics.description: To lose = be deprived of; to loose = release from fastenings; to loosen = make less tight or ease a restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loose conveys idea of complete release; loosen, partial release.

rubrics_metrics.name: luxuriant vs luxurious
rubrics_metrics.description: Luxuriant = lush, grows abundantly; luxurious = lavish, extravagant, comfortable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'a luxuriant head of hair' vs 'a luxurious resort'. Note this confusion is an instance of catachresis.

rubrics_metrics.name: mad vs angry
rubrics_metrics.description: Mad used to mean 'insane' but has long also meant 'angry'; avoid 'mad' for 'angry' in formal writing due to stigmatization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although common in everyday use, many avoid it in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: majority (countability and verb agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Majority preferably denotes countable things (a majority of votes cast) and use 'most' when appropriate; verb agreement varies by sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When meaning 'preponderance of votes cast,' majority takes a singular verb; when referring to a predominant group, it can take singular or plural depending on construction. If followed by a genitive with a plural object, typically use plural verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: malevolent vs maleficent
rubrics_metrics.description: Malevolent describes an evil mind wishing to harm; maleficent describes desire by the miscreant to accomplish evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'with malevolent intent' vs 'maleficent bullying.'

rubrics_metrics.name: mankind vs humankind
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider using 'humankind' instead of 'mankind'.

rubrics_metrics.name: mantle vs mantel
rubrics_metrics.description: Mantle = long loose garment or metaphorical role (assuming the mantle of a martyr); mantel = structure around a fireplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'family pictures on the mantel'.

rubrics_metrics.name: masterful vs masterly
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterful = dominating, imperious; masterly = having mastered a craft, authoritative (often used of a product of mastery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because masterly makes an awkward adverb, prefer 'in a masterly way.' See also cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: may vs might
rubrics_metrics.description: May expresses what is possible or factual; might suggests uncertainty, hypothetical, or contrary-to-fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I may have turned off the stove' vs 'I might have won the marathon if I had entered.'

rubrics_metrics.name: medal vs meddle vs metal vs mettle
rubrics_metrics.description: Medal = award; metal = substance; to meddle = interfere; mettle = character/courage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use each distinct word in its proper sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: media vs mediums
rubrics_metrics.description: In scientific or mass-communication contexts, plural of medium is usually 'media' and should take plural verb; for spiritualists, plural is 'mediums'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although 'media is' is seen, plural use 'media are' is recommended. Example: 'some bacteria flourish in several types of media'.

rubrics_metrics.name: memoranda vs memorandums
rubrics_metrics.description: Both plural forms are correct, but memoranda has predominated; do not use memoranda as if singular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'this memorandum is' and 'these memoranda are.'

rubrics_metrics.name: mete out
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'mete out' to mean 'to distribute' or 'assign' (mete out punishment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common error: 'meet out' and wrong past tense 'meeted out'.

rubrics_metrics.name: minuscule (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Minuscule = very small; often misspelled 'miniscule'. In printing, minuscules are lowercase letters, majuscules are uppercase.

rubrics_metrics.name: mistreatment vs maltreatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Mistreatment = more general term; maltreatment = harsh form involving rough/cruel handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: mitigate vs militate
rubrics_metrics.description: To mitigate = lessen/soften effects; to militate = have a marked effect on (usually followed by 'against'). Avoid 'mitigate against' for correct 'militate against.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'mitigating circumstances lessen the seriousness of a crime' vs 'his nearsightedness militated against his ambition.'

rubrics_metrics.name: moot vs mute
rubrics_metrics.description: Moot traditionally = debatable or (modern) having no practical significance; mute = silent/speechless (offensive as noun 'deaf-mute').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pronunciations: moot (/moot/), mute (/m[y]oot/). Examples: 'a moot point' vs 'deaf-mute' (avoid).

rubrics_metrics.name: much vs very
rubrics_metrics.description: Much generally intensifies past-participial adjectives and some comparatives; very intensifies adverbs and most adjectives including certain past-participial adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'much obliged', 'very carefully', 'very bored'. See referenced section 5.90.

rubrics_metrics.name: murder vs manslaughter vs homicide
rubrics_metrics.description: Murder and manslaughter are unlawful killings; murder is malicious and intentional. Homicide includes lawful killings and can refer to the killer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'murder is done maliciously and intentionally'.

rubrics_metrics.name: myself (pronoun misuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'myself' in place of I or me; use reflexively or emphatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: correct reflexive 'I did myself a favor'; don't use 'myself' after 'and' as a substitute. Also see 5.51.

rubrics_metrics.name: naturalist vs naturist
rubrics_metrics.description: Naturalist = person who studies natural history; naturist = nature worshipper or nudist.

rubrics_metrics.name: nauseous vs nauseated
rubrics_metrics.description: Nauseous traditionally means 'causing nausea'; nauseated means 'feeling nausea'. Avoid ambiguous 'nauseous' for 'nauseated' in formal use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer participial adjectives 'nauseated' and 'nauseating' to reduce ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: necessary vs necessitous
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary = required under the circumstances; necessitous = impoverished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the necessary arrangements' vs 'living in necessitous circumstances'.

rubrics_metrics.name: neither (usage and agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four points: (1) as subject, takes singular verb; (2) neither-nor should frame grammatically parallel expressions; (3) simple neither-nor should have only two elements (though multiple 'nor' acceptable for emphasis); (4) pronunciation acceptable either /nee-thar/ or /nt-thar/.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given for each point.

rubrics_metrics.name: noisome
rubrics_metrics.description: Noisome means noxious, offensive, or foul-smelling, not related to 'noise'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'a noisome landfill'.

rubrics_metrics.name: none (verb agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'None' may take singular or plural verb. Guideline: if followed by singular noun, treat as singular; if by plural noun, treat as plural. For emphasis, singular verb with plural noun is allowable though possibly stilted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'none of the building was painted' vs 'none of the guests were here'.

rubrics_metrics.name: nonplussed
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally means 'surprised and confused'; now often misused to mean 'unfazed'. Avoid the newer usage and variant spelling 'non plused'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also 'faze'.

rubrics_metrics.name: notable vs noticeable vs noteworthy
rubrics_metrics.description: Notable = readily noticed (applies to qualities and physical things); noticeable = detectable with the senses; noteworthy = remarkable, deserving attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'notable sense of humor', 'a noticeable limp', 'a noteworthy act of kindness'.

rubrics_metrics.name: notwithstanding (spelling and alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: One word. Less formal alternatives: despite, although, in spite of. 'Notwithstanding' may precede or follow a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show position variation: 'notwithstanding her bad health' and 'her bad health notwithstanding'.

rubrics_metrics.name: observance vs observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observance = obedience to a rule/custom; observation = watching or a remark based on watching/studying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the family's observance of Passover' vs 'a keen observation about the defense strategy'.

rubrics_metrics.name: obtuse vs abstruse
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtuse describes a person who can't understand; abstruse describes an idea that is hard to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person who is obtuse is dull-witted; abstruse = incomprehensible or nearly so.

rubrics_metrics.name: odious vs odorous vs odoriferous vs malodorous
rubrics_metrics.description: Odious = hateful/extremely unpleasant; odorous = detectable by smell; odoriferous has meant both fragrant and foul; malodorous = smelling quite bad. 'Odiferous' is mostly jocular and not recorded in most dictionaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't misuse 'odious' for smell-related meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: avoid needless 'of' phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'of' needlessly after words like all, off, inside, outside; prefer shorter constructions (e.g., June 2015 rather than June of 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To improve style, remove of-phrases you can reasonably delete.

rubrics_metrics.name: off + of (usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Never put 'of' after 'off' when 'off' functions as preposition/adverb (we got off the bus).

rubrics_metrics.name: officious
rubrics_metrics.description: Officious = aggressively nosy, meddlesome, overeager to tell people what to do; not related to 'officer' and not to be confused with 'official'.

rubrics_metrics.name: on vs upon
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'on' to 'upon' unless introducing an event or condition; 'upon' is acceptable in certain formal constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'put that on the shelf' vs 'upon the job's completion, you'll get paid.' For more about 'on', see 'onto'.

rubrics_metrics.name: oneself (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Oneself' is one word, not 'one's self'.

rubrics_metrics.name: onto vs on to vs on
rubrics_metrics.description: Onto implies movement and is a preposition; 'on' can be an adverb in verb phrases with 'to' as a preposition. A trick: mentally insert 'up' before 'on' — if it still makes sense, 'onto' is likely right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'jumped onto the bars' vs 'held on to the bars' vs 'good on the parallel bars' (no motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: oppress vs repress
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppress = persecute/tyrannize (more negative); repress = restrain or subordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: or (subject agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'or' joins singular nouns functioning as subjects, use a singular verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'cash or online payment is acceptable'.

rubrics_metrics.name: ordinance vs ordnance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinance = municipal regulation/authoritative decree; ordnance = military armament/weapons and ammunition.

rubrics_metrics.name: orient vs orientate
rubrics_metrics.description: To orient = get one's bearings; 'orientate' is a poor variation unless used in the sense 'to face or turn to the east.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'it took the new employee a few days to get oriented to the firm's suite.'

rubrics_metrics.name: ought vs should
rubrics_metrics.description: Both express duty; 'ought' is stronger and requires a fully expressed infinitive (do not omit 'to').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'you ought not to see the movie.' Don't omit 'to' after 'ought'.

rubrics_metrics.name: outside (use of 'of')
rubrics_metrics.description: In spatial references, don't use 'of' after 'outside' (outside the shop); 'outside of' is acceptable colloquially for 'except for' or 'aside from.'

rubrics_metrics.name: over as 'more than'
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'over' to mean 'more than' is acceptable idiomatic English.

rubrics_metrics.name: overly (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the word 'overly' as it's not the best usage; prefer 'over-' prefix (overprotective) or 'unduly'.

rubrics_metrics.name: pair (number and agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Pair' is singular; plural is 'pairs'. 'Pair' may take singular or plural verb depending on sense/construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'this pair of sunglasses was on the table' vs 'the pair were inseparable'.

rubrics_metrics.name: palette vs palate vs pallet
rubrics_metrics.description: Palette = artist's board or colors used; palate = roof of mouth or taste; pallet = wooden platform or crude bed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mnemonic associating '-er' in stationery with paper for stationery elsewhere; here, remember distinct senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: parameters (avoid pretentiousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although it sounds elegant/scientific, 'parameters' is often pretentious in nontechnical contexts; prefer boundaries, limits, guidelines, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: partake in vs partake of
rubrics_metrics.description: Partake in = participate; partake of = get part of or have a quality to some extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'partake in class discussions' vs 'partake of the banquet'.

rubrics_metrics.name: partly vs partially
rubrics_metrics.description: Both mean 'to some extent'; 'partly' is preferred in that sense. 'Partially' also means 'incompletely' or 'unfairly' (biased).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'partly responsible' vs 'partially cooked' vs 'he treats his friends partially'.

rubrics_metrics.name: past vs passed
rubrics_metrics.description: Past can be adjective, noun, preposition, or adverb; passed is past tense/participle of 'pass'. Avoid using 'sunk' as simple past incorrectly elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'times past' (postpositive), 'we passed the school'.

rubrics_metrics.name: pastime (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Pastime' is spelled with one 's' and one 't' (pass + time) not 'past time'.

rubrics_metrics.name: peaceable vs peaceful
rubrics_metrics.description: Peaceable = inclined to avoid strife; peaceful = serene, tranquil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'peaceable kingdom' vs 'a peaceful day.'

rubrics_metrics.name: peak vs peek vs pique
rubrics_metrics.description: Peak = apex; peek = quick/illicit glance; pique = fit of wounded vanity or to annoy/arouse interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'pique' to mean 'to arouse interest' (not 'peaks'). Example: 'an article piques one's interest.'

rubrics_metrics.name: pedal vs peddle
rubrics_metrics.description: Pedal relates to foot-operated devices; peddle = try to sell goods (often by traveling) or sell questionable goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'peddling magazine subscriptions door to door'.

rubrics_metrics.name: pendant (noun) vs pendent (adj)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pendant = item of dangling jewelry; pendent = hanging or suspended (adjective).

rubrics_metrics.name: penultimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Penultimate = next to last; should not be used to mean 'ultimate'. 'Antepenultimate' = next to the next-to-last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the penultimate paragraph'.

rubrics_metrics.name: people vs persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional view: 'persons' for small numbers, 'people' for larger, but today 'people' is used for both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'only three people were there'.

rubrics_metrics.name: perpetuate vs perpetrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpetuate = sustain or prolong; perpetrate = commit (often a wrong act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'perpetuate the species' vs 'perpetrate a crime'.

rubrics_metrics.name: personally (usage cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'personally' only to indicate an action done by the person rather than an agent, or to limit considerations; avoid with 'I' when stating opinions (weakens statement) except in special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three points with examples: 'personally signed', avoid redundancy 'The senator personally shook hands', and exception when expressing differing private opinion vs public action.

rubrics_metrics.name: persuade vs convince
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuade associates with actions; convince associates with beliefs/understandings. Both can take that-clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditionally 'persuade to (do)' preferred over 'convince to (do)', but both are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: pertain vs appertain
rubrics_metrics.description: Pertain to = relate directly; appertain to = belong to or concern as a matter of form/function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the clause pertains to assignment of risk' vs 'the defendant's rights appertain to the Fifth Amendment'.

rubrics_metrics.name: peruse
rubrics_metrics.description: Peruse means 'to read with great care' not 'to read quickly or scan'. Don't use as fancy substitute for 'read'.

rubrics_metrics.name: phenomenon vs phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Phenomenon = singular; plural = phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the phenomenon of texting' vs 'cultural phenomena'.

rubrics_metrics.name: pitiable vs pitiful
rubrics_metrics.description: Pitiable = worthy of pity; pitiful = very poor in quality or arousing sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: pleaded vs pled
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Pleaded' is the standard past tense/participle of plead; avoid 'pled'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'he pleaded guilty'.

rubrics_metrics.name: plethora (avoid overuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plethora denotes an excess or overabundance; avoid using it as mere equivalent of 'abundance'.

rubrics_metrics.name: populace vs populous
rubrics_metrics.description: Populace = population as a whole; populous = densely populated.

rubrics_metrics.name: pore vs pour
rubrics_metrics.description: To pore over something = read it intently; don't confuse with 'pour'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'they pored over every word'.

rubrics_metrics.name: practicable vs possible vs practical
rubrics_metrics.description: Practicable = capable of being done (feasible); possible = might be capable of happening/being done but uncertain; practical = fit for actual use/in a particular situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate shading among the three; see 'impractical' cross-reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: precede vs proceed
rubrics_metrics.description: To precede = happen before or go before in sequence and can mean 'to outrank'; to proceed = go on/continue/resume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common misspelling: 'preceed'. Use 'precedence' for the noun sense of outranking.

rubrics_metrics.name: precipitate vs precipitous
rubrics_metrics.description: Precipitate = happening suddenly/rashly (describes actions); precipitous = dangerously steep (describes cliffs/inclines).

rubrics_metrics.name: precondition (prefer alternatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'condition' or 'prerequisite' instead of 'precondition'.

rubrics_metrics.name: predominant (adj) vs predominate (verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predominant = adjective; predominate = verb. Using 'predominate' as an adjective is nonstandard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'a predominant point of view' vs 'a point of view that predominates'.

rubrics_metrics.name: prejudice (verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a verb, 'prejudice' is a legalism; prefer 'harm' or 'hurt' in plain English. 'Prejudiced' as an adjective meaning biased is normal.

rubrics_metrics.name: preliminary to (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'before' or 'in preparing for' rather than 'preliminary to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: presently (ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Presently' is ambiguous between 'now' and 'soon'; write whichever you mean more explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: preventive vs preventative
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Preventive' is strictly correct; 'preventative' is a common corrupt form.

rubrics_metrics.name: previous to (avoid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'before' instead of 'previous to'.

rubrics_metrics.name: principle vs principal
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle = natural/moral/legal rule; principal = person of authority, initial deposit, or adjective meaning 'most important'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the principle of free speech' vs 'a principal role'.

rubrics_metrics.name: process of / in the (delete)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can almost always delete the phrase 'process of' or 'in the process of' without affecting meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: propaganda (meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda = singular noun denoting false/misleading information used to influence people; plural is 'propagandas'.

rubrics_metrics.name: prophesy vs prophecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophesy = verb (to foretell); prophecy = noun (a prediction). 'Prophesize' is erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: proscribe vs prescribe
rubrics_metrics.description: To proscribe = prohibit; to prescribe = say officially what must be done or specify a medical remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'legislation that proscribes drinking while driving' vs 'the doctor prescribed pills'.

rubrics_metrics.name: protuberance (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Protuberance is spelled without an extra 'r' despite temptation from 'protrude'.

rubrics_metrics.name: proved vs proven
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Proved' is preferred past participle of 'prove'; 'proven' should be used only as an adjective ('a proven success').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'it was proved to be true'.

rubrics_metrics.name: purposely vs purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Purposely = deliberately/on purpose; purposefully = done with a certain goal or clear aim in mind. These are distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An action may be done purposely without being purposefully aimed at a specific result.

rubrics_metrics.name: question whether vs alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Question whether' is traditionally best phrasing; 'question of whether' and 'question as to whether' are phraseologically inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: quick vs quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quickly' is general adverb; 'quick' is properly used adverbially in certain idiomatic phrases (get rich quick, come quick).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also referenced section 5.160.

rubrics_metrics.name: quote vs quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditionally 'quote' is a verb; many use 'quote' as noun informally, reserving 'quotation' in formal contexts. Journalists often distinguish 'quotes' as contemporary remarks and 'quotations' as pithy wisdom-of-the-ages lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: rack vs wrack
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Rack' covers many nouns/verbs and is standard in familiar senses; 'wrack' is standard only for seaweed/kelp noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'rack- ing his brain', 'wrack of seaweed'.

rubrics_metrics.name: raise vs raze
rubrics_metrics.description: Raise = elevate/bring up; raze = demolish/level to the ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'we raised some money' vs 'they razed the building'.

rubrics_metrics.name: reason (usage 'reason why' and 'reason ... is that')
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) 'reason why' is centuries old and acceptable when 'reason that' is not adequate; (2) prefer 'reason ... is that' over 'reason ... is because.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the reason we returned on July 2 is that we wanted to avoid hordes of tourists'.

rubrics_metrics.name: recur vs reoccur
rubrics_metrics.description: To recur = happen again and again or return to attention/memory; to reoccur = merely happen again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate different senses: 'his knee problems recurred' vs 'the leak reoccurred'.

rubrics_metrics.name: reference vs referral
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference = source of information/person providing information/authority for assertion; referral = directing someone to another person or relegating a matter to another body for recommendation/resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Reference' can also be an attributive adjective ('reference book'). It's not universally accepted as a transitive verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: refrain vs restrain
rubrics_metrics.description: To refrain = restrain yourself/keep from doing something (self-discipline); to restrain = other people stopping you, often by force. One can restrain oneself (self-restraint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'if you don't refrain from disorderly conduct, the police will restrain you'.

rubrics_metrics.name: refute
rubrics_metrics.description: To refute = prove that a statement or idea is wrong—not merely deny or rebut.

rubrics_metrics.name: regrettable vs regretful (and adverb)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regrettable = unfortunate or unpleasant; regretful = a person feeling sorry or disappointed. The adverb 'regrettably' is the synonym of 'unfortunately' (not 'regretfully').

rubrics_metrics.name: rein vs reign
rubrics_metrics.description: Rein (usually pl.) controls a horse; reign = state/term of dominion. Use 'rein' in idioms 'take the reins' and 'rein in'. Use 'reign' in 'reign of terror' and 'reign supreme.'

rubrics_metrics.name: relegate vs delegate
rubrics_metrics.description: Relegate = assign to a lesser position; delegate = authorize a subordinate or choose someone to do a job/represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'was relegated to desk duty' vs 'Congress delegated environmental regulation to the EPA'.

rubrics_metrics.name: repellent vs repulsive
rubrics_metrics.description: Both mean driving others away; 'repulsive' has stronger connotations of being so disgusting as to make one feel sick.

rubrics_metrics.name: repetitive vs repetitious
rubrics_metrics.description: Both mean 'occurring over and over'; 'repetitive' is fairly neutral, 'repetitious' connotes tediousness inducing boredom.

rubrics_metrics.name: restive vs restful
rubrics_metrics.description: Restive = dissatisfied or bored and impatient for change; restful = peaceful, quiet, conducive to relaxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: reticent (avoid misuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reticent = unwilling to talk about what one feels or knows (taciturn). Avoid using it as a synonym for 'reluctant'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'the representative became uncharacteristically reticent'.

rubrics_metrics.name: rob vs steal
rubrics_metrics.description: Both mean wrongfully take something; 'rob' usually includes threat or act of harming (often to the person being robbed).

rubrics_metrics.name: role vs roll
rubrics_metrics.description: Role = acting part or way involved/influence in activity; roll = roster, something made by rolling, cylinder shape, or verb meaning to rotate/wrap/move forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples clarify uses: 'the role of Hamlet' vs 'guest roll', 'roll over!'

rubrics_metrics.name: sacrilegious (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct spelling is 'sacrilegious' (related to 'sacrilege'), avoid switching letters around the root.

rubrics_metrics.name: seasonal vs seasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: Seasonal = happening as expected during a time of year or relating to seasons; seasonable = timely or fitting the time of year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'snow skiing is a seasonal hobby' vs 'seasonable motions for continuance'.

rubrics_metrics.name: sensual vs sensuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensual = indulgence of the physical senses, especially sexual; sensuous = aesthetic enjoyment (avoid hack-writer salacious use).

rubrics_metrics.name: sewer vs sewage vs sewerage
rubrics_metrics.description: Sewer = wastewater pipe; sewage = waste carried by such a pipe; sewerage = the sewer system as a whole and the function of disposal/treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: shall (legal drafting guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Shall' is little used in everyday North American English; in legal contexts it appears ambiguously and has been widely litigated—legal drafters are advised to avoid it in favor of must/is/will/may, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See references to Garner's legal writing works for collection of authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: shear vs sheer
rubrics_metrics.description: Shear = cutting tool or force affecting movement; sheer = semitransparent, 'nothing but', or almost vertical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'sheer curtain', 'sheer madness', 'a sheer cliff'.

rubrics_metrics.name: shine (intransitive vs transitive past tense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intransitive 'shine' past tense is 'shone' (the stars shone); transitive 'shine' past tense is 'shined' (the caterer shined the silver).

rubrics_metrics.name: sight vs site
rubrics_metrics.description: Sight = something worth seeing or a device to aid the eye; site = place physical or electronic. The phrase 'set one's sights' means focus on a goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also 'cite'.

rubrics_metrics.name: simplistic
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Simplistic' means oversimplified and has derogatory connotations; don't confuse with 'simple'.

rubrics_metrics.name: since (time vs causation)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Since' may relate to time or causation; causal 'since' existed before Chaucer. Use 'because' if there's potential confusion with temporal sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'since I'm a golfer' as causal.

rubrics_metrics.name: sink (inflection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflected sink-sank-sunk; avoid using 'sunk' as simple past (the ship sunk).

rubrics_metrics.name: slew vs slough vs slue
rubrics_metrics.description: Slew as noun = many/lots (pronounced /sloo/); slough (noun) = swamp; as verb, to slew = turn/slide violently; 'slue' is variant in American English. Past tense 'slew' corresponds to 'slay' (Cain slew Abel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spellings/pronunciations vary; be aware of contexts and forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: slow vs slowly (adverb choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'slowly' as the general adverb; 'slow' can be used adverbially in colloquial pithy statements or injunctions ('go slow!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also 5.160.

rubrics_metrics.name: sneak (regular conjugation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugate 'sneak' as sneak-sneaked-sneaked; reserve 'snuck' for dialect or tongue-in-cheek usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: space (figurative use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'space' as a vogue equivalent of 'area' is current but avoid it in formal writing; prefer 'area'.

rubrics_metrics.name: spit (different senses, conjugations)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'spit' means 'to expectorate' the inflection is spit-spat-spit; if 'to skewer', it's spit-spitted-spitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show difference: 'he spat a curse' vs 'the hens have been spitted for broiling'.

rubrics_metrics.name: stationary vs stationery
rubrics_metrics.description: Stationary = immobility; stationery = writing materials (paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memory aid: associate -er in stationery with paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: staunch vs stanch
rubrics_metrics.description: Staunch = adjective 'ardent and faithful'; stanch = verb meaning 'to stop the flow' (American English). In British English 'staunching the flow' is standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'a staunch supporter' vs 'stanch the bleeding'.

rubrics_metrics.name: strait vs straight
rubrics_metrics.description: Strait = narrow channel or difficult position (also in compounds like 'straitlaced'); straight = unbent, steady, candid, honest, or heterosexual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'dire straits' vs 'straightforward' senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: strata (plural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strata is plural of stratum; keep it plural and avoid double plural 'stratas'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Fussell identified nine discrete strata'.

rubrics_metrics.name: strategy vs tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategy = long-term plan to achieve a goal; tactic = short-term method for immediate limited success. Strategy may involve several tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note 'stratagem' spelling distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: such (avoid legalese)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'such' to replace 'this' or 'that' can be symptomatic of legalese and is often no more precise; it's acceptable to use 'such' with mass nouns or plurals when meaning 'of that type'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'such impudence' and 'such vitriolic exchanges'.

rubrics_metrics.name: supersede (spelling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct root leads to 'supersede' (not 'supercede'); avoid the variant 'supercede'.

rubrics_metrics.name: systematic vs systemic
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematic = according to a plan or organized method; systemic = affecting the whole of something (esp. physiological) or analogous systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'systemic problems within the corporate hierarchy'.

rubrics_metrics.name: sneak (listed again)
rubrics_metrics.description: (See 'sneak' earlier) Use regular conjugation; reserve 'snuck' for dialectal/tongue-in-cheek.

rubrics_metrics.name: take vs bring (see)
rubrics_metrics.description: (Cross-reference present: 'take. See bring.')
